analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: Senator DeMint's bill to make the Bush tax cuts permanent and repeal the estate tax got zero cosponsors and died on the Senate calendar without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have removed the expiration dates written into the 2001 and 2003 tax-cut laws, making every provision of those laws permanent — including the top income tax rate and the 15% rate on dividends and capital gains [S2][S3]. It also would have permanently repealed the estate tax, per the bill's own title [S3], and made alternative minimum tax relief permanent through a phased-in exemption [S2][S3]. It was introduced in the final weeks of the 111th Congress, never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsor, and died when the Congress ended [S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the largest tax savings would have gone to the highest-income households: permanent low rates on top incomes, a permanent 15% rate on dividends and capital gains, and — uniquely — total elimination of the estate tax, which only applies to estates above an exemption threshold worth several million dollars at the time. Middle-income families would also have benefited from permanence of the child tax credit, marriage penalty relief, and the alternative minimum tax patch.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and multimillion-dollar estates

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sunset clause of the 2001 tax law, making all of its provisions — including the reduced top income tax rates — permanent rather than expiring after 2010 [S2][S3].
Repeals the sunset on the 2003 law's reduced tax rates on dividends and capital gains, locking in the 15% rate permanently [S2][S3].
Permanently repeals the estate tax, as stated in the bill's title and purpose [S3].

Phases in higher alternative minimum tax exemption amounts from 2010 through 2020 and permanently allows certain nonrefundable credits (child tax credit, adoption credit, savers' credit and others) to offset the AMT [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the cost of making all the tax cuts permanent instead of letting them lapse, which means the revenue gap is carried by future taxpayers through added debt or absorbed through reduced government spending. Because the largest dollar benefits flow to the highest incomes and the largest estates, the permanent tax code the bill would create is less progressive than one where the upper-income provisions expire.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Treasury, through added debt and lost revenue

drawbacks.text: Making every provision permanent removes the ability to let the high-end rates expire on schedule; a permanent extension of the full package costs vastly more over a decade than a temporary one, because the largest provisions never sunset [S2][S3].
Estate tax repeal exclusively benefits estates above the exemption threshold — at the time, estates worth several million dollars — while forfeiting the revenue those estates would otherwise pay.
The bill would have terminated the Affordable Care Act's increased tax benefits for adoption after December 31, 2011, a benefit cut buried inside a tax-extension bill [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The middle-class pieces — the child tax credit, marriage penalty relief, and the AMT patch — were broadly popular and kept many families from owing the AMT. But the bill bundled them with its most expensive and least broadly shared provisions: permanent high-end rate cuts and full estate tax repeal. Permanence, rather than a temporary extension, locked in the full long-term cost of the entire package and removed the option of revisiting the top rates later. The adoption-benefits sunset was a straight loss with no offsetting purpose stated in the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate's final weeks, read twice, placed on the calendar, and never called up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim DeMint (R-SC) introduced the bill on November 18, 2010, and no senator cosponsored it [S4][S5].
The bill would have removed the expiration dates in the 2001 and 2003 tax laws, making their provisions permanent, including the reduced rates on dividends and capital gains [S2][S3].
The bill's stated purpose included permanently repealing the estate tax [S3].

It would also have phased in a higher alternative minimum tax exemption through 2020, made AMT relief for certain credits permanent, and ended the Affordable Care Act's enhanced adoption tax benefits after 2011 [S2][S3].

It was read the second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 651) on November 19, 2010; no committee action, floor debate, or vote followed, and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill itself, since it never advanced. The concentrated interests it targeted — top earners and large estates — did not get the permanence it offered, and the public was spared a vote on permanently extending the full high-end package at its maximum cost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; the bill went nowhere

for.name: Sen. Jim DeMint
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar in the final weeks of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill up for floor action; it sat on the calendar until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls occurred and the bill had no cosponsors, so the partisan shape can only be inferred from its single Republican sponsor; it never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill's biggest items flow to the top: permanent low top income tax rates, a permanent 15% rate on dividends and capital gains, and full estate tax repeal, which only multimillion-dollar estates would ever use. The cost is forgone federal revenue that ordinary taxpayers ultimately bear through debt or reduced spending [S2][S3].
Repealing the 2003 law's sunset locks the 15% rate on dividends and capital gains in permanently; these income types are concentrated among higher-income filers [S2][S3].

Families also keep the lower rates, larger child tax credit, marriage penalty relief, and — through the AMT patch — protection from the alternative minimum tax, which would otherwise have grown to hit many middle-income filers [S2][S3].
